facts: At 10:04 UTC, checkout failure rate increased from 0.4% to 9%.
Database latency increased at approximately the same time as the checkout failure spike.
The external payment provider reported intermittent errors.
The incident evidence explicitly states the root cause is not confirmed.
assumptions: That 'approximately the same time' for the database latency increase means within a few minutes of 10:04 UTC (exact timestamp not given).
That dep-1842 was deployed to a service in the checkout critical path (not explicitly stated).
That the payment provider's reported errors overlap in time with the 10:04 UTC spike (exact timing of provider report not given).
That the 0.4% baseline and 9% failure figures are measured consistently (same metric definition/source before and after).
That no other concurrent changes (e.g., config changes, infra maintenance, traffic spikes) occurred in this window.

hypotheses.claim: Deployment dep-1842 introduced a defect that caused the checkout failure spike.
supporting_evidence: dep-1842 completed at 10:01 UTC, only ~3 minutes before the 10:04 UTC failure spike, suggesting temporal proximity.
A code/config deployment is a common cause of sudden step-change failure rate increases.
contradicting_evidence: No evidence provided that dep-1842 touched checkout, database, or payment-related code paths.
Database latency and payment provider errors offer alternative explanations not necessarily linked to the deployment.
No rollback or canary data presented to confirm the deployment's causal role.

hypotheses.claim: Increased database latency caused (or contributed to) the checkout failure spike.
supporting_evidence: Database latency increase coincided approximately with the checkout failure spike.
Checkout flows commonly depend on database reads/writes, so elevated latency could cause timeouts/failures.
contradicting_evidence: 'Approximately the same time' is imprecise; sequencing (did latency rise before or after failures?) is not established.
No data on which database, query patterns, or whether latency rise was within the checkout transaction path.
Could be a downstream effect of the deployment or of increased retries from payment errors rather than an independent cause.

hypotheses.claim: External payment provider intermittent errors caused (or contributed to) the checkout failure spike.
supporting_evidence: Payment provider is a direct dependency for checkout completion; provider-side errors would plausibly manifest as checkout failures.
Provider self-reported intermittent errors, an independent external signal not tied to internal deployment.
contradicting_evidence: No timestamp given for when the provider's errors began relative to 10:04 UTC.
No data on error rate/volume from the provider to assess whether it's sufficient to explain a 0.4%→9% jump.
Could be a symptom rather than a cause, e.g., if internal retries/timeouts (from DB latency or the deploy) are hammering the provider and causing it to also see errors.

hypotheses.claim: Multiple factors (deployment, database latency, payment provider issues) combined or cascaded to cause the spike.
supporting_evidence: All three signals occurred in the same narrow time window, which is consistent with a cascading failure (e.g., deploy causes DB latency, which causes payment timeouts, which causes checkout failures).
contradicting_evidence: No causal chain evidence (e.g., logs/traces) links the three events together.
Coincidental timing does not establish causation or interaction between the three signals.

missing_information: Exact timestamp(s) of the database latency increase relative to 10:04 UTC and to dep-1842's completion.
Exact timestamp(s) of when the payment provider began reporting/experiencing intermittent errors.
Contents/scope of dep-1842 (which services/components, config vs. code change, feature flags).
Whether dep-1842 has been rolled back or a canary/control comparison exists.
Error logs or traces from checkout service showing failure reasons (timeout, 5xx from payment provider, DB error, etc.).
Which database(s)/tables/queries experienced latency increase, and whether they are in the checkout critical path.
Payment provider's own incident status/timeline and affected regions or transaction types.
Whether checkout failure rate correlates more strongly with DB latency, payment errors, or neither (statistical/temporal correlation analysis).
Traffic volume changes around this time (to rule out load-driven causes).
Any alerts, config changes, or infra events (e.g., autoscaling, network) in the same window not yet reported.
reversible_next_actions: Roll back dep-1842 in a controlled manner (or disable via feature flag) and observe whether checkout failure rate and DB latency return to baseline — fully reversible and provides causal signal.
Pull and review checkout service error logs/traces for the incident window to classify failure causes (timeout, DB error, payment gateway error) — non-invasive, read-only.
Correlate precise timestamps of DB latency metrics, payment provider error reports, and dep-1842 deployment/rollout completion on a single timeline — read-only analysis.
Query the database's slow-query log/APM to identify which queries/services drove the latency increase and whether they are called by checkout — read-only.
Contact the payment provider for their detailed incident timeline and affected transaction scope to compare against internal timestamps — non-invasive.

If safe, temporarily route a small percentage of checkout traffic away from the payment provider (if an alternate provider/fallback exists) to test provider-error hypothesis — reversible if fallback exists.
Check for autoscaling/infra events or traffic spikes around 10:01–10:04 UTC to rule out load-based causes — read-only.
Set up/verify dashboards showing checkout failure rate, DB latency, and payment provider error rate on one view for ongoing monitoring during investigation — non-invasive.

uncertainty.reason: Only coarse, approximate timing is available for three candidate contributing signals (deployment, DB latency, payment provider errors), with no confirmed sequencing, magnitude data, or causal linkage (e.g., logs/traces) between them. The evidence explicitly states root cause is unconfirmed, and multiple plausible independent or cascading hypotheses remain equally consistent with the facts given.
